name: Ptosis surgery for asymmetry

card.summary: Eyelid-lifting surgery to correct a drooping upper lid so the eyes match; an established procedure, with uneven lids a recognised complication.
card.note: Evidence covers ptosis repair generally; asymmetry results can recur or be uneven after surgery.

quick.overview:
Ptosis is a drooping upper eyelid. Surgery tightens or replaces the lifting mechanism, and in looksmaxxing discussions it is cited as a way to make a droopy lid match the other eye.

Surgical series describe it as an established treatment for mild to severe ptosis, but outcomes vary by cause and technique.
quick.mechanism: Techniques include shortening the levator muscle, resecting Muller's muscle, or suspending the lid from the forehead muscle (frontalis sling) when the lid muscle is very weak.
quick.risks: Reported complications include uneven lids after surgery, dry eye if the eye does not close fully, bleeding, infection, rarely loss of lid movement, and recurrence.

lead: Ptosis is drooping of the upper eyelid, caused by dysfunction of the levator muscle, its nerve supply, or the sympathetic supply to Muller's muscle. Causes include aging, congenital factors, trauma and underlying conditions such as myasthenia gravis.[1] Ptosis surgery for asymmetry refers to repairing a lower-set lid so that the two eyes look more alike.

Surgical options include levator resection, Muller's muscle resection and frontalis or Whitnall slings.[1] Published case series of minimally invasive suspension techniques report correction of mild and moderate ptosis with short recovery.[2]
infobox: Levator resection, Muller's muscle resection, frontalis sling, Whitnall sling [1]
0.1% oxymetazoline drops, FDA-approved 2020 for acquired ptosis [1]

paras: Ptosis is classified as neurogenic, myogenic, aponeurotic, mechanical or neurotoxic; pseudoptosis describes apparent drooping caused by poor lid support or a higher lid on the opposite side.[1]

Levator resection is generally used when levator function is 5 mm or less, and Muller's muscle resection is another option. A frontalis sling is described as preferred in oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy and considered most effective for moderate to severe congenital ptosis, while a Whitnall sling is often chosen when cosmetic appearance is the priority.[1] Children are usually not operated on until about age 4 or 5.[1]
A 2019 series described minimally invasive conjoint fascial sheath suspension for mild to moderate unilateral or bilateral blepharoptosis, intended to shorten recovery and avoid conspicuous scars.[2]

Complications include uneven eyelids after surgery, dry eyes if closure is incomplete, bleeding and infection, and rarely loss of lid movement. In one study cited on Wikipedia, half of patients needed further surgery within 8 to 10 years.[1]

Published case series of ptosis correction exist, including a 2019 study of conjoint fascial sheath suspension for blepharoptosis.[2] Eyebrow position is also described as a factor evaluated in cosmetic and reconstructive surgery.[3] No studies found on ptosis surgery specifically framed as looksmaxxing asymmetry correction.

timeline.event: FDA approves 0.1% oxymetazoline eye drops for acquired ptosis.[1]
